title: Cochrane Handbook Chapter 14: Completing 'Summary of findings' tables and grading the certainty of the evidence

extracted.subtask_short: Grading certainty that evidence supports an effect claim
extracted.subtask_description: Operationalizes the GRADE approach for meta-analytic (pooled) evidence, deciding whether synthesized evidence actually supports a stated effect estimate/conclusion and how confidently, via five downgrading domains and three upgrading criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty of evidence definition
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The extent to which one can be confident that an estimate of effect or association is close to the quantity of specific interest.' A 'supported' claim is one where the reviewers can be confident the reported number (or direction) is close to the true quantity, not merely one where a number was computed from the included studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study-design starting point (RCT high, NRSI low)
rubrics_metrics.description: Randomized trials begin at HIGH certainty. Non-randomized studies of interventions (NRSI) begin at LOW certainty by default, reflecting inherent confounding and selection-bias risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using the ROBINS-I risk-of-bias tool, all studies may start at 'high' and NRSI are still expected to typically fall two levels once bias is accounted for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-level certainty rating (high/moderate/low/very low)
rubrics_metrics.description: High (⊕⊕⊕⊕): few/no concerns across domains, very confident true effect close to estimate. Moderate (⊕⊕⊕◯): downgraded one level, moderately confident, true effect likely close but could be substantially different. Low (⊕⊕◯◯): downgraded two levels, confidence in the estimate is limited. Very low (⊕◯◯◯): downgraded three levels (the floor), very little confidence in the effect estimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of bias downgrade domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Classified as 'no serious limitations' (no downgrade), 'serious limitations' (downgrade one level), or 'very serious limitations' (downgrade two levels). Specific concerns for randomized trials: failure to generate a proper random sequence, lack of allocation concealment, inadequate blinding (especially for subjective outcomes), large loss to follow-up (attrition above roughly 50% warrants consideration of a two-level downgrade), and selective outcome reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translating from a structured risk-of-bias tool: 'low risk of bias' across studies → no downgrade; 'some concerns' unlikely to lower confidence → no downgrade; 'some concerns' likely to lower confidence → downgrade one level; 'high risk of bias' with one crucial limitation → downgrade one level; 'high risk of bias' substantially weakening confidence → downgrade two levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistency (heterogeneity) downgrade domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Downgrade when there is unexplained heterogeneity that affects interpretation of the estimate - i.e., wide variation in effect estimates across studies without a plausible explanation. Assessment relies on the I² statistic (qualitatively 'not important,' 'moderate,' 'substantial,' or 'considerable'), the Chi² test and tau, confidence-interval overlap across studies, and variation in point estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not downgrade when heterogeneity is explained by identifiable subgroups (consider separate Summary of Findings tables for clearly different populations instead of downgrading), or when only a single study contributes to the outcome (rate inconsistency as 'none,' not 'not applicable').

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirectness downgrade domain (indirect comparison and PICO mismatch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two distinct kinds: indirect comparison (no head-to-head trials of A vs. B exist, only A-vs-placebo and B-vs-placebo trials, requiring an indirect comparison) and PICO mismatch (the evidence addresses a narrower or different version of the review's question - a different population, a different intervention delivery, a suboptimal comparator, or surrogate/disease-oriented outcomes standing in for the patient-important outcome actually being claimed). Assess each PICO element separately, then classify as 'no indirectness' (no downgrade), 'serious indirectness' (downgrade one level), or 'very serious indirectness' (downgrade two levels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision rule is to make explicit, documented judgments about whether the population/intervention/comparator/outcome differences materially change whether the studied evidence still supports the target claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imprecision downgrade domain (Optimal Information Size)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses an Optimal Information Size (OIS) threshold logic: if the 95% CI excludes a risk ratio of 1.0 and the total number of events/participants exceeds the OIS, precision is judged adequate. Downgrade when: the sample size/event count is below the OIS; the CI includes both appreciable benefit and appreciable harm; or the CI is wide enough to cross clinically important thresholds. Rough guides: RR thresholds of <0.75 or >1.25 for 'appreciable' effects, roughly 400 events as a traditional minimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly flagged as a misapplication: downgrading for imprecision merely because there are 'few studies' rather than because the CI/event-count is actually inadequate. A single study can still be evaluated for imprecision via the OIS criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication bias downgrade domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Downgrade when there is an asymmetric funnel plot suggesting missing (usually negative or null) studies, selective non-reporting of outcomes across the included studies as a set (distinct from within-study selective reporting, which belongs under risk of bias), an unusually large number of small studies not contributing data to an outcome, or a 'prototypical' red flag pattern such as multiple small, industry-funded studies all reporting favorable results. Serious evidence downgrades one level; strong/serious evidence downgrades two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upgrading criteria for non-randomized evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Large effects (RR > 2 or < 0.5 supports a one-level upgrade if no plausible confounders explain the association and estimates are consistent and precise; RR > 5 or < 0.2 supports consideration of a larger upgrade). Dose-response gradient (a clear monotonic relationship between exposure level and outcome). Opposing plausible confounding (if all plausible biases would be expected to work against the observed effect, the true effect is probably at least as large as observed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked examples: bicycle helmets reducing head-injury risk (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.26-0.37) upgraded to moderate certainty despite an observational design; bleeding risk rising with INR and cardiovascular risk of rofecoxib rising with dose (RR 1.33 at <25 mg/day vs. 2.19 at >25 mg/day) as dose-response examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: MECIR conduct standard: justify every up/downgrade decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Cochrane's MECIR conduct standards require: use all five GRADE considerations for every reported outcome; explicitly justify every downgrade/upgrade decision in the review's text and Summary of Findings footnotes; and have two independent reviewers assess and reach consensus on certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same evidence base can support different claims at different certainty (worked example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Worked example (compression stockings for DVT prevention): symptomless DVT, low-risk population, RR 0.10 (95% CI 0.04-0.26), 2637 participants/9 studies → High certainty (no downgrades). Superficial vein thrombosis, RR 0.45 (95% CI 0.18-1.13), 1804 participants/8 studies → Moderate certainty (downgraded for imprecision). Oedema, mean difference -4.7 (95% CI -4.9 to -4.5), 1246 participants/6 studies → Low certainty (downgraded two levels: unvalidated and unblinded outcome measurement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same body of studies can support different claims (different outcomes) at very different certainty levels, and the downgrade rationale must be traceable to specific, named domain concerns rather than a global impression.
